cards.explanation: The answer is wail. The verse says, “Wail, O cypress, for the cedar has fallen…” (Zechariah 11:2). The cedar was the big tree of the forest, and when it goes down, the trees around it are told to cry out. Nobody in that forest is feeling chipper. This is a sad moment for Lebanon, friends.

The answer is False. The cedars aren't alone in this. The cypress is told to wail, and so are the oaks of Bashan, because “…the dense forest has been cut down!” (Zechariah 11:2). The whole forest is caught up in it, friends.

The young lions roar because the thickets of the Jordan are destroyed. The verse says, “…the thickets of the Jordan are destroyed.” (Zechariah 11:3). A thicket is thick growth along the river, and I think that's the kind of place a lion calls home. So the roar is about a ruined thicket.

The answer is a flock marked for slaughter, and it's a heavy job, friends. The LORD says, “Pasture the flock marked for slaughter…” (Zechariah 11:4). This flock is already headed for slaughter. Even so, the prophet is told to shepherd it.

The sellers bless the LORD because they are rich, and listen to how they say it. They say, ‘Blessed be the LORD, for I am rich!’ (Zechariah 11:5). They sell the flock and walk away calling themselves rich. It's an uncomfortable verse, friends, and I think it's meant to be.

The answer is True, and that's the sad part. The text says, “Even their own shepherds have no compassion on them.” (Zechariah 11:5). The ones who are supposed to look after the flock don't have any compassion for it. That's a lonely spot for sheep, friends.

The answer is his neighbor and his king. The LORD says He will “…cause each man to fall into the hands of his neighbor and his king, who will devastate the land…” (Zechariah 11:6). Those are the hands the verse names, friends.

The answer is afflicted. The text says, “So I pastured the flock marked for slaughter, especially the afflicted of the flock.” (Zechariah 11:7). The buyers, the sellers and the shepherds give the flock no mercy, and the prophet gives special care to the afflicted. That lines up well with a God who watches out for the hurting.
The answer is False. The prophet says, “My soul grew impatient with the flock, and their souls also detested me.” (Zechariah 11:8). It's mutual, friends. Nobody is happy in this pasture.
The answer is that he stops shepherding them. He says, “I will no longer shepherd you.” (Zechariah 11:9). He's done with the job. It's a hard moment, friends, and I think it hurts.

The answer is the covenant with all the nations. The prophet cuts the staff called Favor in two, “…revoking the covenant I had made with all the nations.” (Zechariah 11:10). The staff is named Favor, and snapping it ends that covenant. The cut means something, friends.

The answer is True. The text says, “…the afflicted of the flock who were watching me knew that it was the word of the LORD.” (Zechariah 11:11). The afflicted are the same ones the prophet pastured especially back in verse 7. They watch the staff get cut, and they know it's from the LORD.

The answer is False. The prophet says, “If it seems right to you, give me my wages; but if not, keep them.” (Zechariah 11:12). He leaves the decision to them, friends. Then they weigh out thirty pieces of silver.

The answer is the potter. The LORD says, “Throw it to the potter…” (Zechariah 11:13). The silver goes to a potter, not to anyone else. I'd have a lot of questions about that order, friends, but the prophet just does it.

The answer is False. The prophet says, “So I took the thirty pieces of silver and threw them to the potter in the house of the LORD.” (Zechariah 11:13). He does exactly what the LORD says. The silver doesn't stay in his hands, friends.

The answer is the brotherhood between Judah and Israel. The prophet says, “Then I cut in two my second staff called Union, breaking the brotherhood between Judah and Israel.” (Zechariah 11:14). The staff is named Union, and when it's cut, the brotherhood breaks. The second snap matters as much as the first, friends.

The answer is False. The LORD says this shepherd “…will neither care for the lost, nor seek the young, nor heal the broken, nor sustain the healthy…” (Zechariah 11:16). He doesn't heal the broken, friends. The list gets heavier from there.

The word is devour. The LORD says this shepherd “…will devour the flesh of the choice sheep and tear off their hooves.” (Zechariah 11:16). A shepherd is supposed to protect the flock, and this one takes from it. It's a hard picture, friends.

The answer is that he deserts the flock. The message ends, “Woe to the worthless shepherd, who deserts the flock!” (Zechariah 11:17). A shepherd who walks away from the flock leaves the sheep alone. That's a heavy way to end, friends.
